Matthew 6
MATH-yoo SIX
proper noun (passage)
Matthew is the first of the four Gospels in canonical order; its placement reflects the early church's recognition of its connection to the Old Testament as the “Gospel of the Kingdom” — the systematic presentation of Jesus as the fulfillment of Messianic prophecy and the inauguration of the New Covenant. Chapter 6 is the second of three chapters comprising the Sermon on the Mount (Matt 5–7); it focuses on three practices of Jewish piety (almsgiving, prayer, fasting) corrected from performance for human approval toward sincere communion with the Father, and concludes with the foundational kingdom priority statement.

Biblical Definition

Matthew 6 is the kingdom-priorities chapter of the Sermon on the Mount, addressing the three classical practices of Jewish piety — giving, praying, and fasting — and then extending to the decisive question of ultimate allegiance: treasures, eyes, masters, and anxiety. The organizing principle is the contrast between the “hypocrites” who practice piety for human approval and the kingdom-citizen who practices piety in the secret place before the Father who sees in secret.

The Lord's Prayer (Matt 6:9–13) is positioned at the chapter's center as the pattern-prayer of the new covenant community: “Pray, then, in this way: Our Father who is in heaven, hallowed be Your name” (Matt 6:9). The prayer establishes divine fatherhood, divine holiness, divine kingdom, and divine will as the primary orientation of prayer before any petition for personal need is made; God's concerns precede our own in the structure of the prayer itself.

The chapter's climactic teaching arrives in verses 25–34: “For this reason I say to you, do not be anxious for your life, as to what you shall eat or what you shall drink — nor for your body, as to what you shall put on” (Matt 6:25). The ground of the command against anxiety is not positive thinking but the knowledge of the Father: the One who clothes the lilies and feeds the sparrows is the Father of those who seek His kingdom. The culminating priority is absolute: “But seek first His kingdom and His righteousness — and all these things shall be added to you” (Matt 6:33). Kingdom and righteousness first; provisions follow from the Father's hand as a matter of covenant care, not human striving.

Webster 1828 Definition

Matthew 6: the sixth chapter of the Gospel according to Matthew; the second of three chapters of the Sermon on the Mount; contains the Lord's Prayer (vv. 9–13), the three-fold correction of Jewish piety from performance for approval to sincere communion with the Father, and the foundational kingdom-priority command (“seek first His kingdom and His righteousness”, v. 33).

MATTHEW, GOSPEL OF: The first of the four canonical Gospels; author the apostle Matthew (Levi the tax collector, Matt 9:9); written primarily to Jewish readers, presenting Jesus as the King-Messiah who fulfills the law and the prophets.

Chapter 6 is the ethical heart of the Sermon on the Mount: three corrections to hypocritical piety (almsgiving, 6:1-4; prayer, 6:5-15; fasting, 6:16-18), followed by the teaching on treasures (6:19-21), the single eye (6:22-23), the impossibility of two masters (6:24), and the resolution of anxiety in kingdom-seeking and Father-trust (6:25-34).

The Lord's Prayer (Matt 6:9-13) has been the primary pattern-prayer of the Christian church from the first century; its structure — God's concerns before our petitions — is the constitution of Christian prayer.

Key Scripture

Matt 6:9 — "After this manner therefore pray ye: Our Father which art in heaven, Hallowed be thy name."

Matt 6:25 — "Therefore I say unto you, Take no thought for your life, what ye shall eat, or what ye shall drink; nor yet for your body, what ye shall put on. Is not the life more than meat, and the body than raiment?"

Matt 6:33 — "But seek ye first the kingdom of God, and his righteousness; and all these things shall be added unto you."

Matt 6:34 — "Take therefore no thought for the morrow: for the morrow shall take thought for the things of itself. Sufficient unto the day is the evil thereof."

Modern Corruption

Modern readings of Matthew 6:33 (“seek first His kingdom”) reduce the kingdom to personal spiritual growth or social justice programs, losing the eschatological and covenantal register of the Matthean “kingdom of heaven” that Christ inaugurated and will consummate.

expand to see more

The “kingdom of God” in Matthew's Gospel is not a metaphor for inner transformation or a social program for the present age but the cosmic reign of the Son of David, inaugurated in the first coming of Christ and to be consummated at His return — a reign that encompasses the whole created order, not merely the private spiritual lives of its citizens. To reduce “seek first His kingdom” to “prioritize your personal spiritual disciplines” domesticates the Matthean kingdom-theology into a therapeutic framework; to reduce it to “engage in social justice activism” strips out the eschatological consummation that gives the present seeking its urgency and direction. The kingdom of the Sermon on the Mount is the kingdom that comes with power and that the Father gives to His little flock (Luke 12:32).

The prosperity-gospel reading of Matthew 6:33 treats “all these things will be added to you” as a prosperity promise: seek God first, and material abundance follows. But Christ's context is the anxiety of those who lack food and clothing — and His promise is not abundance but sufficiency: the Father knows what His children need (Matt 6:32), and He provides according to His wisdom, not their wish-list. The “all these things” added are the necessities of life, not the luxuries of comfort; and they are added by the Father's governance, not produced by the believer's faith-formula.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Matthew 6 draws from the Psalms, the prophets, and the wisdom tradition to present the kingdom-citizen's primary orientation: God-ward in prayer, single-eyed in loyalty, Father-trusting in provision.

expand to see more

Greek basileia (βασιλεία) — kingdom, royal reign; the central concept of Matthew's Gospel (appearing over fifty times as “kingdom of heaven”); not primarily a place but a reign — the active, sovereign governance of the King-Messiah over every sphere of creation, inaugurated at the first coming and to be consummated at the second

Greek merimnao (μεριμναω) — to be anxious, to be divided in concern (from merizo, to divide + nous, mind); anxiety is a divided mind that assigns its energy to multiple competing concerns rather than the single primary concern of the kingdom; the word appears five times in Matthew 6:25–34, making anxiety-vs-kingdom-seeking the structural tension of the passage

Hebrew shema' — hear, obey; the Deuteronomy 6 command to love God with the whole heart, soul, and strength is the Old Testament antecedent to Matthew 6:24–33; the “two masters” impossibility and the “seek first” command are both applications of the Shema's demand for undivided loyalty to the one Lord

Greek haplous (απλούσ) — simple, single, generous; used in Matthew 6:22 for the “single” eye that fills the body with light; the image is of an eye focused on one thing — a spiritual single-mindedness that corresponds to the undivided loyalty of the whole-hearted servant and the whole-hearted kingdom-seeker

Usage

"The Heidelberg Catechism's exposition of the Lord's Prayer (Q&A 118–129) unpacks the six petitions of Matthew 6:9–13 as the complete structure of Christian prayer: adoration, submission to divine will, daily need, forgiveness, protection, and ascription of glory — establishing that prayer shaped by Matthew 6 is not a list of personal requests but the alignment of the soul with the concerns and priorities of the Father."

"Calvin's exposition of Matthew 6:25–34 in the Institutes (3.7–10) and in his Gospel commentary treats the anxiety commands as the practical application of the doctrine of providence: the believer who truly knows the Father's governance of all things — including the sparrow and the lily — finds the rational basis for non-anxiety in the character of the God who governs, not in the circumstances that appear threatening."

"The Puritan William Perkins in his Treatise of the Vocations (1603) applied Matthew 6:33 to Christian engagement with ordinary work: the kingdom-seeker does not despise daily labor but frames it within the primary orientation of the kingdom, so that every vocation is exercised as a service of the King rather than a means of self-securing against the anxieties of the coming day."
